newsitem.title: UK: FUND VIEW-Invesco sees Japan on upward track.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW-Invesco sees Japan on upward track.

text.p: It has been a hard ride for Japanese equities, but Invesco Tokyo Trust thinks fundamental values will be rewarded in the end.
"Its the laggard market world wide," Invesco general manager James Hegarty told Reuters.
"It can only get better. It's under-bought and its immune to an interest rate rise, which is something that can't be said for other equity markets in the world."
Invesco recently upped its asset allocation to Japan to 19.5 percent of a global equity portfolio, against a benchmark figure of 17 percent.

Pointing to the very narrow gap between yields on 10-year Japanese government bonds and shares -- currently just 12.5 bps -- Invesco believes that the market could be ripe for a change in investor sentiment.
"All we need now is good numbers over the next three months to convince investors that a change of sentiment is appropriate," said Hegarty.

As of the most recent reporting period, the year to May 31, 1997, the trust has outperformed its benchmark Tokyo exchange TOPIX index -- an 18.5 percent loss in net asset value (NAV) versus a 22.3 percent loss in TOPIX.
But the three months to the end of June have seen a 23 percent rise in NAV, versus an 18.9 percent jump in TOPIX. The trust has a market cap of 49 million sterling.
Invesco Tokyo Trust is bullish on the electric appliance and communication sectors, according to director Ritsu Matsushita, and continues to be underweight in financial services.
"Last year the Tokyo market was two-tiered -- only exporting companies like Honda and Sony made historic highs," Matsushita said.
"I think that now those kind of pure exporters have been nearly fully discounted and we'd like to switch from pure exporters to more diversified global manufacturers like Fujitsu and NEC."
"On the other hand we underweight banks substantially because bad loan problems are still serious," Matsushita said.
The fund uses a top-down approach for sector selection combined with bottom-up stock picking within sectors.
On the macroeconomics front, Invesco expects the recent sharp rise in Japanese gross domestic product to prove to be a one-off prompted by consumer spending to beat a consumption tax rise in April.
"What is going to recur is that public demand will detract from GDP," said Hegarty.
That would be bad news for the construction sector, which is highly dependent on government spending.
Pharmaceutical shares could also be hit, as the government tries to shift the burden of prescription medicine onto consumers.
In the medium to long term, Invesco sees several factors that could produce better fundamentals for Japanese equities.
One is Japanese pension funds, which are highly regulated and tend to carry a relatively small proportion of their assets in equities.
Invesco expects pension regulations to be eased and for pension fund flows to provide a useful floor for shares.
Matsushita thinks that a small number of Japanese companies are bringing on board shareholder value concepts.
"The higher return on equity (ROE) of ten years ago was the result of growth of Japanese economy. The important thing now is changing the attitude and the priority of management."
"Before the priority was employees and growth and exports and now it should be ROE and the interest of shareholders," he said.
